en: Padminī Ratnarakṣita Chapter 27 Nagoya Takaoka CA17, 41v2–42r2; input by PDSz, 9.iii.2025, Kolozsvár [The text begins with the following verses: Just as a lotus born from the mud does not become defiled by that very mud, so too, though born from the world, the wise one is not defiled by the world. Just as the sun, having risen, dispels the darkness of the night, so too, having arisen in the world, he dispels the darkness of ignorance. Just as the moon, free from clouds, shines with great splendor in the sky, so too, free from the clouds of afflictions, he shines with the light of wisdom. Just as a lamp placed within a house illuminates all its interior, so too, having entered the city of the body, he illuminates the entire world. Just as a great cloud, laden with water, brings relief to the earth, so too, like a rain-cloud of Dharma, he brings relief to the world of beings. Just as a great physician, skilled in medicine, cures all diseases, so too, skilled in the medicine of Dharma, he cures the disease of suffering. Just as a great caravan leader leads a multitude across the desert, so too, acting as a guide for beings, he leads them across the ocean of existence. Thus, O King, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is a great physician, a great caravan leader, a great protector, and a great refuge for all beings. Therefore, you should honor him with all your heart. [End of fragment]

He speaks for the purpose of answering the question regarding the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*), beginning with the word "therefore" (*ata*). "Kāma" refers to the thirteenth [vowel]. "Rudra" refers to the eleventh. "Randhra" refers to the ninth. "Muni" refers to the seventh. "Bāṇa" refers to the fifth. "Rūpa" refers to the first. It should be understood that the word "tuta" follows "Agni. "Agni" refers to the third [vowel]. "By way of instruction" (*upadeśataḥ*) means starting from the first square of the row consisting of thirteen squares; this is the instruction. "Of the first square" (*prathamakoṣṭhasya*) means of the row of the first square.

"Regarding the fifth": this refers to that which is situated in the fifth square. "One should cause it to be placed above by means of the first square" means that one should place upon it that which is situated in the first square within that very same row of squares. This is also the case in some readings where it says "by means of a single square. Then, when the multiplication is performed, the syllable *oṃ* shall result.

In order to provide an answer to the extraction of the mantra, it is said: "From this," and so forth. "Desire" refers to the thirteenth; "fierce" refers to the eleventh; "aperture" refers to the ninth; "sage" refers to the seventh; "arrow" refers to the fifth; and "form" refers to the first—this is to be understood as the *pāra* (beyond) of fire. "Fire" refers to the third.

Regarding the phrase "from the oral instructions," this refers to the instructions beginning from the first square of the garland consisting of thirteen squares. Regarding "of the first square," this means the section of the first row of squares; "the fifth" refers to that which resides in the fifth square.

Regarding the phrase "the very first square [of the grid] should be placed above," this means that whatever resides in the first square of the first row of the grid should be placed above; such is the meaning. In this regard, even for those who speak of it as being "the single square itself," it is the same. There, having been transformed into a quality, it becomes the syllable OṂ.

Regarding the reading "there, the eleventh": the word "there" (*tatra*) means "from that"; thus, when counting according to the sequence of writing from the square, the letter *aṃ* situated in the eleventh position—when combined with the vowel *u* placed above it—becomes the syllable *oṃ* joined with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). As for the sandhi, it occurs because of its non-existence [in the source]. Then, one should place the third *ma*, in the form of a bindu, upon the half-moon from the row of squares containing the number nine. The remainder is easily understood.

Regarding the expression "by the eleventh square," the phrase "from that" refers to that very [square]; it is the syllable *oṃ* situated in the eleventh position when counting according to the sequence of writing in the squares. By placing it above that, they are made into a single quality, and thus it becomes the *oṃ* syllable together with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). This is due to their very conjunction.
Therefore, one should place the letter *ma* in the form of a bindu upon a half-moon in the third cell of the third row of the grid of nine numbers. The remainder is easy to understand.

In this regard, first is the ten-syllable heart-mantra of the Blessed One; then the seven-syllable subsidiary heart-mantra; then the thirteen-syllable heart-mantra of the Goddess; and then the four-line mantra. Thus should the extraction [of these mantras] from the Guru be understood.

Here, first is the ten-syllable heart mantra of the Bhagavān; then follows the seven-syllable near-heart mantra; then the thirteen-syllable heart mantra of the Goddess; and then the four-line mantra. The extraction of these should be learned from the Guru.

He states the employment [of the mantra] for one who has thus concealed it: "From the book," and so forth. He states when this extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*) should be performed: "On the tenth day," and so forth. He states that the distinction between the mantra and the deity is a violation of the pledge (*samayabhraṃśa*), and that such a thing must not be done: "Better," and so forth. He dispels the disparagement of wisdom (*prajñā*): "Arising from the left," and so forth. Regarding "the libation and consumption with the left": the libation and the consumption are performed with the left hand.

Thus, the hidden intention was spoken in the passage beginning with "the book" (*glegs bam*). When should these mantras be extracted? It is said: "The tenth," and so forth. Regarding the division of mantras and deities, it is a violation of the samaya; therefore, it should not be done. This is stated in the passage beginning with "life-force" (*srog*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "one who disparages wisdom abandons [it] among worldly people," and so forth: "Leftover food and left-hand eating" means that one eats leftover food with the left hand.

It prevents the abandonment of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). Regarding the passage beginning with "five" and so forth: "freed from all conceptual constructions" (*sarvasaṅkalpavinirmukta*) means that which is established by the initial conceptualization regarding all phenomena that are empty of beginning, middle, and end. "Free from all dualities" (*sarvadvandvavivarjita*) means one who does not perceive a distinction between the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the five Tathāgatas. It dispels disrespect toward the guru. Regarding the passage beginning with "the guru" and so forth: the passage beginning with "all" and so forth is an epithet of the guru.

By this, "abandon the root transgressions" refers to how many of the fourteen root transgressions indicated in the *Sekapaṭala* have been specified; however, all those mentioned in other tantras should be understood [as well], such as the prohibition against abandoning great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the five families, and so forth. "Completely liberated from all conceptual constructions" means being free from conceptualizations regarding the beginning, middle, and end of all phenomena that are empty of such [distinctions]. "Second, having utterly abandoned everything..."

Thus, one should not differentiate between the five aggregates and the five Tathāgatas. Regarding the abandonment of disrespect for and disparagement of the guru, [the text says] "the guru" and so forth; "all" and so forth are the specific qualities of the guru. By these, the root downfalls are completely abandoned.
Thus, one should understand not only as much as is indicated by the fourteen root downfalls taught in the *Abhiṣeka-paṭala*, but also all those taught in other tantras.
Namely:
contempt for the true gurus, transgressing the commands of the Perfectly Awakened One,
speaking of faults against one's true brothers with anger, and being devoid of great loving-kindness.
The projection of any one of the three vehicles, the disclosure of secrets to those who are not yet ripened,
and doubt regarding the Buddha-nature, the aggregates, and intrinsic purity.
But when the beginning, middle, and end of "corrupt friendliness" and so forth are empty, there are two types of conceptualization.
Furthermore, the conceptualization of those [objects] is indeed that very conceptualization;
it is the abandonment of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) and the defiling of the faithful mind.
The fourteenth is disparaging women despite having attained the pledge;
upon any one of these transgressions, purification occurs through re-initiation.

[42r] Root downfall: namely, to show contempt for the sublime guru; to transgress the word of the Perfect Buddha; to speak of the faults of one’s brothers out of anger; to utterly abandon great loving-kindness; to completely renounce the mind of awakening; to disparage the other three vehicles; to proclaim secrets to those who are not mature; to disparage the aggregates as being the Buddha himself; and to doubt the purity of intrinsic nature.

To be loving toward the wicked in the beginning, middle, and end; to conceptualize emptiness here and there; to corrupt the minds of those endowed with faith; and not to rely on obtaining [the teachings] according to the samaya—these fourteen are "censuring women. For any of these downfalls, one must again purify them through empowerment. These are the root downfalls.
The forceful seizing of wisdom, likewise the seizing of the thought of awakening,
the secret concealment from those who are unfit, and dispute within the assembly circle.
In a funeral feast (śrāddha), there is otherwise a discourse on Dharma; for seven days, the disciples remain [there].
To falsely pride oneself on being a yogi and to preach the Dharma where there is no faith—[these are faults].
Thus, these eight gross offenses (sthūlāpatti) are to be confessed according to the prescribed rule;
by this, the sequence for a gross transgression of the root [offense] when one has fallen [into it] is to be understood.

Holding that with the power of wisdom, and likewise holding the mind of awakening; not concealing [the teachings] from those who lack the fortune for the secret; quarreling within the assembly of the mandala; giving Dharma discourses to those other than the faithful; staying among the śrāvakas for seven days; being a liar while a yogi; and teaching the Dharma to those without faith—these are the eight faults of the *poma* (stūpa).
"If it has been impaired, one should confess; this is to be understood from the ritual procedure. This is the sequence for the root and gross offenses."
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-seventh chapter. [curl] ||
This is the explanation of the twenty-seventh chapter.
